clinicalPearls: Presents as acute dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, hypertension and features of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema during or shortly after transfusion
It is essentially hydrostatic pulmonary oedema caused by an inability to accommodate the transfused volume
Raised jugular venous pressure and a positive fluid balance help distinguish it from lung injury
Natriuretic peptide levels are typically elevated, reflecting cardiac strain, in contrast to acute lung injury
Risk is greatest in the elderly, in small patients, and in those with cardiac or renal impairment
Management is to stop or slow the transfusion, sit the patient upright, give oxygen and administer diuretics
It responds to diuresis, which is the key clinical distinction from transfusion-related acute lung injury
Prevention rests on slow transfusion rates, single-unit prescribing and consideration of prophylactic diuretics in at-risk patients
reference.pathophysiology: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload results from the intravascular volume of a transfusion exceeding what the circulation can accommodate. In patients with limited cardiac reserve or impaired renal handling of fluid, the added volume raises left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing fluid across an intact alveolar-capillary membrane into the alveoli. The oedema is therefore hydrostatic and cardiogenic in nature, accompanied by raised filling pressures and cardiac strain that elevate natriuretic peptides. Rapid infusion rates, large volumes and pre-existing cardiac or renal disease are the principal contributors, and because the mechanism is volume-related the process reverses with diuresis and reduction of the circulating load.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from decompensated heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging showing pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly and upper-lobe blood diversion
Natriuretic peptide levels, typically raised, to support a cardiogenic mechanism
Assessment of fluid balance and jugular venous pressure
Echocardiography to evaluate ventricular function and filling pressures
Arterial blood gas or oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia
Renal function to gauge fluid-handling capacity
redFlags: Acute breathlessness with hypertension and raised jugular venous pressure during transfusion
Rapidly progressive hypoxaemia in an elderly or fluid-overloaded patient
Frank pulmonary oedema requiring urgent oxygen and diuresis
Failure to improve with diuretics, prompting reconsideration of lung injury
reference.prognosis: Recognised promptly and treated with diuresis and respiratory support, most patients recover quickly, but it is a common and under-recognised cause of transfusion-related morbidity and death, particularly in frail patients with cardiac disease.
pitfalls: Confusing it with transfusion-related acute lung injury and withholding the diuretics that would help
Transfusing at excessive rates or in multiple units where a single unit would suffice
Overlooking the elderly and small patients who are most vulnerable to volume overload
Ignoring a raised natriuretic peptide and pre-existing cardiac history when assessing dyspnoea
management: Stop or slow the transfusion at once and sit the patient upright when acute dyspnoea and hypertension develop during or after a component
Give supplemental oxygen and loop diuretics to offload the hydrostatic pulmonary oedema, with nitrates as an adjunct for severe cardiogenic oedema
Escalate to non-invasive ventilation such as continuous positive airway pressure for refractory hypoxaemia
Monitor fluid balance and cardiac status, treating this as a volume-overload state that reverses with diuresis

Prevent in at-risk patients by transfusing single units slowly and spread over time, with pre-emptive diuretic cover and restrictive thresholds, especially in the elderly, small patients and those with cardiac or renal impairment
Report the reaction to the transfusion service and review future transfusion planning
